For the information of hon.
members I table copies in English and French of an exchange of notes between Canada and the United States as to an agreement respecting Unemployment Insurance. subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION

speechtext: On the order for second reading of senate bills:

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext: By arrangement it was agreed that private bills should be taken first to-day. A large number of divorce bills appear on pages 16, 17, 18, 19 and 20 of the order paper. Two of the bills on the list are not divorce bills. If it is the pleasure of the house I will call all the divorce bills together.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I am going to repeat the protest we have made each year when this procedure has been followed. If this were not a time of war we would insist that these bills be read and adopted separately, not because we are opposed to divorce but because we are opposed to this method of dealing with divorce cases. The thing is both a tragedy and a farce. Here we have a long list of bills to be considered and given second reading together, and I suppose very few members of the house know anything whatever about them. It is true that a small committee of this house gives these bills a cursory examination after a senate committee has looked into them. It is a blot upon the entire institution of parliament and the alleged progressiveness of a civilized country such as this that we should deal in this way with the dissolution of marriage. It is a grave responsibility for members of this house to assume. We undertake it lightly, and it becomes simply a formality. I want to protest against it as strongly as I can, and to reassert our belief that this is a matter which ought to be decided by the courts after proper inquiry into the grounds submitted for the dissolution of the marriage. If the present laws are inadequate, with regard to grounds and other matters, then the laws should be amended in order to modernize our whole procedure in this very grave matter.
I just want to add that if I am here when peace returns, I shall feel it my duty to see to it that each of these bills is read separately and every item of the bills discussed on the floor of the house. The sooner we get some agreement with the provinces concerned with regard to the granting of divorces, the better it will be for the good name of this parliament and of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a good deal to commend in certain portions of the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). To lump these bills together and pass them en bloc is, of course, just a vacation of the functions of parliament. At the same time we are endeavouring to conserve time, and perhaps no great harm is being done.
The whole thing comes back to the underlying procedure. These bills should not be here at all. Parliament has gone part way; we have arranged to set up divorce courts in certain jurisdictions in this country where there were no divorce courts in days gone by. In other jurisdictions there were divorce courts; we never had divorce bills from my own province, for instance. But parliament; should go the whole way. I do not see how anyone could object to the establishment of divorce courts in certain jurisdictions in this country, instead of continuing the present system, under which these bills go through as a matter of course and, in my view, in many instances without being properly considered. Certainly no attention is given to them in this house, and I doubt very much if attention is given to them in the private bills committee. I have not been a member of that committee for many years, but if any attention is given to them at all I think it must be just a matter of form. Occasionally a fight develops in connection with some particular case, where interested parties come, meet the members and put forth their points of view. Under such circumstances a fight will sometimes develop.
But this principle, this whole system, is wrong. The time of parliament should not be

Procedure in Divorce Legislation
taken up with the consideration of bills of this kind. We delegate many matters to the courts. We delegate questions of contested elections to the courts. We have gone part way in respect to jurisdiction concerning divorce. Parliament should go the whole way, and the government should step in and give a lead in that policy.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join my leader in expressing my strong disapproval of disposing of these bills in this way, and of dealing at all in the House of Commons with divorce cases, either singly or in bulk. I understand there are divorce courts in' most of the provinces-in fact, in all of them except two. Surely divorce courts might now be set up in those provinces, and thus remove a blot upon the functions of this parliament.
To-day we have this situation:	A number
of public bills have been passed over for several sessions of parliament. There stands on the order paper in my name, a bill which was introduced in 1940. It has appeared on the order paper at each session, and has been laid aside. Yet that bill is one of great public importance, because it has to do with the health of the people of this country. The domestic difficulties of individuals which result in divorces are not matters of any concern to the rest of the people of Canada. It is their own business. Let them go to the usual places, namely the courts of law, and there settle their differences. I must object most strenuously to the setting aside of bills of great importance to the people of Canada while we rush through the passage of a large number of divorce bills.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is our own fault if we are looking into these cases. In the committee we have a pile of divorce bills a foot high, and when you have read one you do not want to read any more. But we should not open the door wider for those who wish to get out of marriage wedlock, unless we narrow the door through which they come. If a young couple have a cigarette lighter, a little car and a rented suite, I suppose the leader of the opposition would say they have a perfect right to get married.
I would like to see the upper house take the whole marriage question into consideration. It should discuss how, when and under what conditions young folks may be married, so as to build up a stable and Christian home. They should have something to build on. But if we open the door and let them out easy, then we let them in easy as well. The whole matter should be discussed and legislation introduced. Not only should the divorce

question be thought out and laws enacted, but there should be reconsideration of the marriage law as well. Get married in a hurry, love for a little while and away they go. That is not the way to build up a Christian home in this Canada of ours, because the Christian home is the bulwark of Canadian citizenship and of civilization generally.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions hon. members in this corner of the house have voiced sentiments which seem to be in perfect harmony with expressions of opinion this afternoon by hon. members who have spoken. I was somewhat alarmed when it was announced by Mr. Speaker that by special arrangement these bills were to be placed before us this afternoon, and that they are to go through all together. I was not aware of that arrangement having been made, but perhaps that is my fault. I suggest, however, that we should have some little notice when such action is to be taken, because in the minds of some there may be the necessity of discussing one or more of these bills.
In my short experience in attending six regular sessions of parliament I have not yet heard a discussion of one of these divorce bills, taken by itself. I suppose the reason is that we have reached a point in parliament where divorce bills are just ground out from the mill. A certain procedure, which has become more or less stereotyped, has been followed. One reads the evidence of one case, and he has the facts of almost all of them, because they are all about the same.
Nevertheless, having read the evidence in some of these cases, I am a little disturbed at the almost exactly similar way with which each is dealt. It is disturbing to me, because I cannot help thinking that people are commencing to know the way to get a divorce, if they want one. I protest against that.
I do not know if I should say anything respecting the difference between the senate divorce committee and courts of law. I do not know personally the gentlemen comprising that committee. Perhaps some of them are lawyers, but I do feel that a court judge, with his knowledge of court procedure and his examination of evidence, is more competent and more fully qualified to deal with divorce.
I agree with other hon. members in the view that we have reached the point in our history where, in my opinion, the province ol Quebec should take the lead in the matter of referring its divorce bills to a proper court of law. What is to be the procedure with respect to these fifty-one divorce bills? Are they to go through now, all together?

Procedure in Divorce Legislation

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot let this entire series of divorce bills be carried through without voicing my opposition to so reprehensible a practice. Like the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), I believe that parliament is not qualified to pass judgment in such matters of private interest. They should be referred to the courts of those provinces who wish to legislate on the dissolution of marriage. At any event, as Catholics, we are absolutely opposed to divorce because it is contrary to the fundamental principle of Christian ethics. The fact that parliament is called upon to decide in these divorce cases places us in a very false position, as everyone understands. For us, therefore, the principle of divorce is reprehensible, and that under which the House of Commons is called upon to pass a whole series of divorce bills without knowing any of the reasons brought forth to substantiate these petitions, is an even more reprehensible practice and one to which I must voice my opposition.
Mr. LIGUORI LACOMBE (Laval-Two
Mountains) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I fully share the views expressed by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy), and I myself cannot refrain from protesting vigorously against the wholesale carrying of these divorce bills. Divorce is reprehensible in its very essence. On behalf of my electors and in the name of the great majority of the citizens of my province, I wish to protest once more against the carrying of these bills.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to the remarks just made on this divorce question by the two French-speaking members who preceded me. Briefly, here is the procedure followed in the matter: A petition is addressed to the senate with a view to obtaining a bill of divorce. Witnesses are called before the senate divorce committee. The two parties can be represented by counsel and have their witnesses testify. The senators decide
whether or not there are sufficient grounds or evidence of adultery, and they grant or refuse the divorce. These bills then come before the House of Commons, where they are read a first and second time. They are then referred to the private bills committee for consideration, one by one. Returning once again to the house, they are read and considered in committee of the whole, section by section. There is no limit set to their discussion. Then, after a third reading, these bills become law.
In the province of Quebec, almost everyone is opposed to divorce. All Catholics oppose it without exception. The procedure followed in Quebec is one that makes it extremely difficult for the citizens of that province to obtain a divorce; indeed, our legislators believed that the biggest obstacle to divorce they could find was to require the passing of a special act by the dominion parliament. If my hon. friend from Gaspe (Mr. Roy) will only consult the religious authorities in his riding, he will be informed that the clergy of the province of Quebec is opposed to the establishing of divorce courts there. At least that is the opinion of those to whom I have broached the matter.
A divorce case is dealt with by a court like any other case. Divorces are sometimes granted in other provinces in the brief space of fifteen minutes. If the case is ex parte, the judge only hears one side of the story, sometimes only one witness, before granting the divorce at the same sitting. In the province of Quebec, we believe that we can never make the securing of divorces difficult enough, because we do not recognize the principle on which divorce is based, and rightly so to our way of thinking. I should be very astonished to learn that members from other provinces intended to impose in the province of Quebec, which desires only to maintain the status quo, a system of divorce courts such as they have in their own.
I did not intend to speak on this matter to-day, otherwise I might have brought with me quotations to establish'that, in the past, the attitude I have taken has always been that of Catholic representatives of the province of Quebec. And I hold the conviction that we must, as Catholics, insist on the maintenance of the present procedure for obtaining a divorce. We are being asked to allow the second reading of these bills as a whole, but it is not on second reading that their consideration in detail may be undertaken. We are discussing the principle of these bills, but it remains for the private bills committee and the committee of the whole to discuss each case on its merits. I am irrevocably opposed
Private Bills

to divorce and as long as I retain a seat in this house, I shall do my best to make the securing of them as difficult as possible.

Therefore the management of the company felt that it would be wise to have a name of wider application than the name of one of the provinces. I believe there was a company incorporated some twenty odd years ago by this parliament for the purposes of carrying on the business of fire insurance, but up to the present time it has not carried on business. Then of course there is a company incorporated as the Fidelity and Casualty Company of New York. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, May 28, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting

War Appropriation-War Services
to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Usley-Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this committee has spent some time in a discussion of man-power and allied questions. I propose to raise a question of the greatest possible importance in the war effort. I refer to another branch of the minister's department, the bureau of information, and the work it carries on.
It is perfectly obvious that our enemies have taught us a great deal about the power of propaganda and the power of information. They have used it as one of the weapons of war, and although we have a better cause and better institutions we have been slow to make the utmost use of this weapon. It is clear that men buy bonds, make munitions, enlist, fight bravely, bear misfortune, have faith in victory, and give the last ounce that is in them because of their ideas and feelings, but it is particularly true of a country like Canada that it requires an effort of the imagination for the people to understand that this is our war, and an effort of the imagination and knowledge and understanding to appreciate that the best place to defend Canada may be ten thousand miles from our shores, and that the defence of Canada is not the same thing as defence in Canada.
This subject can be considered from three points of view. First, there is the operation of enemy propaganda and counter-propaganda on the enemy and to encourage the people in the occupied countries. Canada can only contribute to the counter-propaganda against the enemy in conjunction with the others of the united nations. Second, there is the use of information to inspire our own people to greater efforts, and I think this committee and this house might quite properly spend some time considering how that can best be done. I propose to limit my present remarks to a third aspect of propaganda, and that is the aspect of our relations with the United States, with our friendly allies, and to discuss how these relations can be improved.
This question has been raised in the house once or twice before, but so far as I am aware it has never been discussed at length. I bring it up now because I have a large number of American friends whom I have seen very frequently since the outbreak of war in the United States and Canada, and I hear them say, with others who have had a similar experience, that we should do more to make our story known in the United States. I think I express the view of every member of this house and of the great majority of the

people of Canada who know anything about it when I say that we should be doing more to make our story known in the United States and to cultivate the best possible relations with her, in the belief that our relations are founded on understanding, and that understanding is founded on knowledge. Persons in the United States say to me when this matter comes up: "Why on earth do you not do more to make the magnificent record of Canada known over here? Why aren't you doing something about it?"
We started the war with every possible advantage. Canada and the United States were the most friendly nations on the face of the earth. The relations between Canada and the United States were closer than those of any other two nations, they were more cordial than those of any other nations. We did not regard the Americans as foreigners, and they did not regard us as foreigners. The relations between Canada and the United States were, as Bruce Hutchison has said, founded on "nature, history, geography, necessity and men's hearts".
It is not too much to say that the whole structure of British-American and allied cooperation was begun in the declarations of President Roosevelt and Mr. King at Wood-bridge and Kingston in 1938, continued through the Ogdensburg declaration of 1940 and the Hyde Park agreement of 1941, and it is no detraction from the magnificent work of President Roosevelt and Prime Minister King to say that the basis for those agreements and for that whole structure of cooperation was the friendly relations of individuals in the United States and in Canada.
This relationship between the United States and Canada has enabled the two countries to cooperate more closely than any two nations have ever done before. We know that in the President of the United States we have a great friend; we know that with the members of his administration Canadians have the closest possible relationship and cooperation. But with President Roosevelt we want to have as friends also the 130,000,000 people who will elect President Roosevelt's successor.
This question is important; it is particularly important now, when we are partners in the greatest adventure the two nations have ever undertaken, and it will continue to be important because the two nations must go down the years together. The future of Canada is bound up in the future of the United States, since we both occupy this north American continent together. Never before has it been more necessary, never before has it been more important, that Canada and Canada's position, work and achievements should be properly

War Appropriation-War Services
understood in the United States. Yet at the present time the ordinary contacts of United States and Canadian citizens are being curtailed by the necessities of war. Last year
14,000,000 United States citizens visited Cam-ada. In ordinary years many hundreds of thousands of Canadians visit the United States. But these exchanges of visits, which produced closer personal relations than have existed between two peoples, are being curtailed because of exchange restrictions, passport and visa requirements, exit permits, and now travel restrictions with regard to gas and rubber. I suggest that we need to watch the undefended boundary line to make sure it does not become a frontier. We need to set a guard not on the border but on our actions to see that measures which may be considered necessary for some immediate purpose do not do far more harm than good in the long run to the friendly relations of the two countries.
Another reason why this matter is pressing now is that the United States itself is, naturally, becoming concentrated on its own war effort, and it will become interested in our work and achievements only in so far as they are news and in so far as that news is promptly presented to the United States.
A third reason is that we know that the enemy is seeking to divide the united nations everywhere he can. I could show you, if I took the time, clippings from United States newspapers indicating a close relationship, much closer than could be accounted for by mere coincidence, between enemy shortwave broadcasts, and the line taken in them, and the line taken in some papers published on this continent. If we do not do enough we shall leave a vacuum into which lies and rumours flow. Where our story is not told there is fertile soil for misunderstanding and rumours. We have seen instances of this. Last year, you will remember when there was a debate in the United States Congress on lease-lend, it was suggested that the Canadian people got cash on the barrel-head for everything they gave to Britain. That story was started and it has been difficult to catch up with. When our friends in the United States learn the extent of Canada's contribution of men-150,000-overseas, and when they think of the United States equivalent, they are amazed. When they hear the full extent of what we have done, I have found that there is a feeling almost of resentment at their not having been told the full story.
I do not suggest that our government should undertake anything in the nature of propaganda or high-powered1 publicity service. What I do suggest is that we should provide machinery for supplying news, because facts bum up rumours and prejudice as the sun bums up fog. I suggest that there is need of that shown even to-day. In the New York Herald-Tribune, a newspaper friendly to Canada, in a recent number following the plebiscite, two United States senators were quoted. One said he was disappointed that "so many people in Canada do not realize the seriousness of this war." Another said he was "glad to see that Canadians had voted to get into the war as we are." I do not suggest that these honourable gentlemen are representative of their people in their lack of knowledge, but it indicates a serious situation when two senators have such a small knowledge of what we are doing as to make statements of this kind. I may tell the committee that in this article those statements are used as a peg on which to hang an exceedingly complimentary and favourable story of what we are doing in the war.
This question has received a good deal more attention in the press of Canada than it has in this house. I suggest that if anyone should know what the true position is, and what the importance of the question is, it is the press of Canada, because they see the United States papers; they clip articles from them; they have contact with the United States press; they know what can be done, and they have a very strong feeling as to what should be done.
I hold in my hand a large number of clippings from Canadian papers expressing their view of this question. The Ottawa Journal says:
There can he little doubt that Canada has suffered considerably in the United States through lack of any coordinated effort on our part to let the American people know what we are doing.
The Toronto Globe and Mail says:
The lack of knowledge in the United States concerning Canada's effort has been exploited by the isolationists with substantial effectiveness.
The Saint John Telegraph-Journal:
We have still a long way to go before our system of information, especially to our American cousins, is satisfactory.
The Family Herald and Weekly Star:
Canada continues to receive a bad press in the United States, and it is high time something was done to tell the American people our story.
In an address delivered before the Canadian club of Montreal, Sir Willmott H. Lewis, Washington correspondent for the London Times, said:
There is not enough Canadian publicity in the United States or in the other American nations. . . .

War Appropriation-War Services
The Montreal Standard says:
Most people in the United States at the present time have no conception of the part Canada is playing in this war.
And again:
Canada is falling dangerously in the esteem of the American people because of the poor impression they have of our war accomplishments.
From the Montreal Star:
We have on several occasions advocated an organized campaign to make the details of Canada's war effort more widely known throughout the United States than they are.
From the San Francisco Chronicle:
The result-
That is, of our failure to give information. 

is that a great and vital story, as vital to us and our way of life as to Canada's goes untold.
It continues:
That is why we wish our Canadian friends were not so gun shy about propaganda. There should be official, recognized agencies of information, telling us at least as much about what the people next door are doing in their war, and our war, as we know from overseas.
From the Minneapolis Star-Journal: Doubtless Canada has been reluctant to carry on in the United States any thorough and systematic effort to make Americans better acquainted with her, lest she be suspected of propaganda for some ulterior purpose.
But it would be a service to Americans if she would do so. It would help to end misconceptions, and to make honest differences of opinion debatable as between friends, not strangers.
The United States and Canada are going to be more and more important to each other, whatever happens in the world. The better they know each other, tile more harmoniously they can work together for the good of both.
Then from the Daily Star, Windsor, Ontario: The American people are actually anxious to hear about Canada's war effort. This is a fact that we have been stressing for some time. It has taken certain persons in authority much too long to realize its truth.
The result has been that, because of timidity about spreading propaganda, Canada has suffered a volume of unjustified criticism.
From the Vancouver Sun:
Canada has been so diffident or incompetent about giving Americans the facts that the Minneapolis Star-Journal finds its readers pitifully ignorant about the whole Canadian situation. Some of them, says the Star-Journal, think that Canada is a dependency of Britain, paying taxes to the British treasury.
The Winnipeg Free Press, commenting on this, says:
The need for an alert, full-time Canadian information bureau in the United States has been apparent for a long time.
And they refer to these United States editorials.
What I suggest is that we should tell our 
story. No one else is going to do it for us. If I may make a constructive proposal it would be that we should have an office in New York. Hon. members may ask, why New York? New York is the centre of publicity, of writers, publications, the publishing business, columnists and radio. It is the place where the people who give the news get the news. This office should be staffed by a small number of people, exceedingly good people, including, in particular, one who would be by experience and qualification well able to meet with Americans and deal with United States publicity agencies. We all know the importance of personal contacts; that there is no field in which personal contacts are more important than this field of public relations. This individual should be a person who knows how public opinion is formed; he should be a Canadian who is in some way representative of the young people of Canada who are fighting overseas.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What would be the hon. member's view as to choosing from the press of Canada a body of men to handle our news, men who have had life experience in publicity?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We have in Canada an able group of pressmen, and I would think that if one or more of them could be attached to this work in the United States it would be very useful. The person whom I have in mind to head the office in New York would not necessarily be a pressman, although he might be one who had had journalistic experience. He would have to be one who is alert to the needs of the modern press. He would have to have the kind of flair that good journalists have for news and how to get it across. What is needed is not an institution, it is a person. He should be the kind of person to whom Americans who make the news will naturally look for assistance and guidance. He should not try to influence public opinion in the United States directly, that would be fatal; he should try to be useful to the people who make public opinion there. He should see that news about Canada gets to the people who can give it to the American people. It would probably be a mistake to have this office attached to the Department of External Affairs, because our diplomatic representatives are used to a slower and more formal manner of conducting business. They have not the instantaneous quickness on the trigger that is necessary to deal with news on the north American continent. By the time anything gets through the diplomatic channels and the Department of External Affairs to the bureau of public information here, the value of the story would be lost; the front pages would have

War Appropriation-War Services moved on to something else. So I suggest that this individual or this office should be attached to the bureau of public information.
Another suggestion is that the minister in Ottawa could work in cooperation with this individual to encourage Canadians who have normal contacts with the United States-and there is a great number of them-to think, when they are making those contacts, of Canada's story and the possibilities' of getting it over to the United States. In fact, every hon. member must be a member of some association, medical association, bar association, trades union, having close associations and affiliations with United States associations of the same kind. All of us can use our natural contacts through these associations to bring home to our United States friends nothing but the facts.
Then, referring to the suggestion of the hon. member for New Westminster, it might also be possible to use Canadian journalists who have friendly associations with journalists in the United States. They might visit them from time to time; a man placed in the middle west might visit his opposite number in the United States middle west and maintain friendly associations with him so that when Canadian news comes to him through the ordinary news channels he would interpret it sympathetically and know the kind of slant to put on it.
I also suggest that this development requires a new attitude in Canada, an attitude whereby we recognize the real importance of this subject and do things in a way to make news. The one really first-class news development which has taken place in Canada, and which has had a continuously good press in the United States, is the work of the wartime prices and trade board. This shows what can be done through the use of good publicity and good publicity men. The fact that we have a price ceiling has from the beginning to date been a matter of news and interest and admiration in the United States.
We need better agencies for getting the news from the places where it is made, that is the fighting fronts, or places in Canada where there are news stories, into the hands of United States agencies. As I said to the house some nights ago, there are magnificent stories of Canadian heroism which have not even been told in Canada yet, and which would be just as useful in cheering our United States friends as in cheering our own hearts. We have reached a stage in the war where deeds count much more than words; where propaganda, stories of action, heroism and achievement, count much more than any speech, and our publicity and information service must be
geared to the task of getting stories from the places where they are made to the places where they are going to do some good. What I suggest is not a loud-speaker in the United States. What I suggest is a pick-up, if I may use a radio term, at the front where the news is made, and a connecting service through to the loud-speaker, which will be the ordinary United States agency which will use the news, if it is news, in the way that agency sees fit.
This, if I may say so, requires a new attitude on the part of our censors. I believe that ever since the beginning of the war stories that might have thrilled our hearts have been left cooling on the desks of censors, and I suggest that the censorship rules should be overhauled and coordinated, to see what can be let through. If it can be let through, send it through quickly, so that it reaches us while the story is still hot. There are stories to be found and to be told of the work of Canadian soldiers, sailors, airmen, the merchant marine and war industries. They are there to be found by people who have a nose for news. They are there to be written by men who can write in an attractive way, and sent back through improved agencies to Canada and thence to our friends in the United States. It is plain enough from stories like those of Larry Robillard and others that brave men are writing tales of heroism with their lives. The records are there; all that is needed is that the records be given a chance to speak for themselves.
I believe the minister himself, if one may gather from rumours abroad some time ago in the public press, is sympathetically inclined toward this idea. I have made these suggestions in the hope of fortifying his inclination, and I want to express my pleasure at the appointment of Mr. Charles Vining to go to the United States to look into this whole question. He is eminently fitted to do so. He has had journalistic experience; he knows the United States, where he has close connections, and I am sure he can make a report on this subject which will be very useful to the government. Whatever that report may be, I cannot help but express my strong conviction that we must do more to tell our story, or see that our story is told, in the United States. We have friends there who want to help us. We have 130,000,000 friends who want to help us. They want to be given the facts; they ask for them. They believe in us; they want to be given the facts to justify their belief. In the long run, relations between countries depend upon relations between individuals, and our relations with the United States will depend upon the relations between individual Americans and individual Cana-

War Appropriation-War Services
dians. Out of tlie last war and our achievements in it Canada achieved a new status and a new standing. I want to see that the exploits of our men in this war stand to Canada's credit also. As Churchill said in 1930, speaking of Canada:
No state, no country, no band of men can more truly be described as the finch-pin of peace and world progress.
I believe that statement may be made true, but it will not be true unless Canada earns and keeps the respect of other countries; and other countries, particularly our United States friends, will have respect for us if they know that we are pulling our full weight in this joint effort.
There is one other aspect of the matter; that is the effect on our own morale. If we continuously read in United States newspapers and in publications such as Life, of the achievements of United States airmen, and we do not see anywhere stories of the achievements of Canadian airmen, then we shall begin to feel that there is something wrong with us. There is nothing wrong with us, but if that continues to happen there will be something wrong with our publicity service. Morale is the most valuable thing in the world, and the least expensive. What more is to be done lies in the hands of the minister and the government, but I have no doubt that the wish of members of this house and of the people of Canada is that something more should be done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have no intention of following the remarks of the hon. member who has just spoken, because in my view the debate on this resolution should be concluded. But I am wondering why he did not give any expression to the feeling of bewilderment that is very evident in the minds of the people of the United States, as expressed in the public press of that country and by individuals of prominence, owing to the fact that this country, which is professing-and I believe in most ways is endeavouring-to carry out a total war effort, as a matter of fact in one particular feature does not have a total war effort. They just wonder over there, and I have seen expression given to this view on many occasions in many United States publications, how in the world this country can have a total war effort if it does not practise total war. There is no doubt that there is a feeling of frustration in the United States with respect to our war effort. They know that our industry is in production; they know that we have a, good army overseas and a good army in training in Canada. Yet they know, from their own experience and

their own example, that according to their standard Canada has fallen down in one particular feature. There is no doubt about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Do they think that of Australia?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Never mind Australia. The United States is our neighbour. They know what we are doing and what we are not doing. In the United States press the plebiscite was greeted as an overwhelming manifestation on the part of the Canadian electors in favour of total war; and when they find that it does not mean total war there is a feeling of bewilderment, to which they have given expression. They will never truly appraise our effort in this war until that position is cleared up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The leader of the opposition has referred to a view that is widely held in the United States and frequently expressed by the people of that country. I wonder if it is expressed as frequently in the United States as it is expressed by certain persons in Canada. I would suggest to the leader of the opposition that he write to the authorities in Washington and ask them for the results of their draft system, in the number of men actually added to the forces since the draft system for compulsory service has been in effect. Get those figures, and then compare them with the number of men we have added to the strength of our armed forces, and my hon. friend will see the comparison.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is just begging the question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is not begging the question at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Give us the figures.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am prepared to say we are raising more men proportionately for our armed forces-

speechtext: By coercion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
No; by a voluntary
method. I do not know why it is that so many people in this country are seeking to decry the value of the voluntary effort.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Because of the back-door method.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is not at all back-door.

speechtext: Certainly it is.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: This, however, is perhaps not the debate in which to discuss that particular question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister, however, does admit that the condition I have indicated prevails in the United States?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, and prevails from a mistaken view of the facts.

-and thereby, if I may say so, doing real harm to the effectiveness of our war effort.
I had not intended making any reference to that point. I expect this whole subject will be fully covered in the debate which will take place within the next few days; and in the course of that debate, in as cool a manner as possible, we can deal with the merits or demerits of compulsory service overseas. I think a strong case can be made for the maintenance of the present system, from the point of view of the effectiveness of the war effort of this country. After all, many of us are concerned with an objective, namely the maximum total aid this country can give in the cause of humanity. We are concerned with the effectiveness of the war effort more than with anything else. I think we shall wish to use that method which will make the greatest contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort, from the point of view of reality, and not from that of theory. I believe the debate which will take place, commencing, I hope, next week, will prove a useful forum for getting down to realities in connection with this subject, and go a long way toward dispelling the heat and frenzy that have grown up in many quarters, in some instances fomented and in other cases as opinions honestly held. We can deal with that question on its merits or demerits.
It was not I who introduced this question directly, but-

speechtext: Before the minister leaves the matter of public information, might I ask, what are the functions of Mr. Paul Reading at Washington.

And never
has been.

At one time, prior to the entry of our great and good neighbour into this conflict, I think the isolationist press in the United States went out of its way to minimize the extent of the Canadian war effort, because the fact that we in Canada had, of our own free will, entered into the war, was the strongest argument against their own position-because we were both north American countries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Oh, well, brush that aside. Did we not enter because this was a British country, and not because we were a north American country?

of the strongest advocates of our participation

May I go back to the situation in the United States. Here we were, two north American countries. We recognized the issues involved. We were both isolationist countries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

The majority of the
people in Canada, prior to 1939, were strongly of an isolationist view.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: Yes, speak for yourself.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think there was much doubt about that. I am perfectly free to say I was one of those who believed it might be possible for north America to hold itself aloof from the quarrels of Europe.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: And let the empire go to the dogs!

That view is one that
cannot now be held by any thinking person.

It never
could, not by any thinking person.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It was a view that I
had abandoned completely before I took part in the debate on Canada's participation in the war. I saw that no free nation could stand alone in this conflict, that all free nations must unite. During the course of that debate I expressed, the view that it would not be long before our great neighbour to the south, in whom the traditions of liberty are deeply ingrained, would enter this conflict. I believe the isolationists thought that Canada's entry into the war was the strongest argument that could be made against their case. If isolationists in Canada could see the light, why should not others who were formerly isolationists also see the light? What the isolationist press in the United States tried to do was to belittle the effort of Canada, and in so doing they received great aid from many Canadian newspapers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What is
an isolationist?

I do not think I should
begin a course of education for the hon. member for Bow River.

speechtext:
It would
be interesting to hear your interpretation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I doubt it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We in Canada have been very careful indeed about our relations with the United States. We have treasured our relations with that country and have desired that they should be as cordial as possible. Our two countries are interdependent upon one another; we share similar traditions and our whole lives are based upon institutions inherited in common from Great Britain. We have been very careful not to indulge in propaganda in the United States. I was greatly impressed by one of the statements made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton), that we in Canada should not tiy to influence United States opinion, that that would be fatal. With that thought in mind, we never, prior to the entry of the United States into the war of her own free will, sought to promote propaganda in the United States. Those who have attempted propaganda in the United States have not increased the cordiality of the relations between that country and the countries of those who engaged in the propaganda.
There is a difference between engaging in propaganda and giving public information as to facts. I am in agreement with much that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has said. Now that we in the northern part of north America are united with our neighbours to the south in a great north American partnership, a new situation is brought about in which it is desirable that they should know as much of our activities as we know of theirs. I was very glad indeed that the Prime Minister was able to announce definitely yesterday that Mr. Charles Vining had been requested to make a survey of the whole situation in the United States, to find out what the attitude of the people there would be in the matter of public information, and make a report on the whole situation. The matter will then be reviewed in the light of the real knowledge that will be brought back, and I am hopeful then that we shall be able to embark upon a policy of public relations and public information as between Canada and the United States that will serve the purpose of enlightening the peoples of the two countries as to the activities of the other without in any way giving offence to either of them.

Madam Chairman, after waiting twenty years it is my extreme pleasure to address for the first time a gracious lady in the chair of this committee.
I wish her many long years of happiness and service in this hon. chamber.
Madam Chairman, it is a rather sad day when a minister of the crown rises in his place at this time of war and attempts to make the people of this country think about isolation and the position of isolationists and how many isolationists there were in Canada a few years ago. No doubt some of them are still here.	.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That was one thing that should not have been raised in this hon. chamber at this time. We have had a sense of frustration, but now another wet blanket has been thrown over us this afternoon. It is not fair to the hon. members of this chamber, it is not fair to you, Madam Chairman, it is not fair to the hon. members who served in the last war and who now surround the Minister of National War Services. I know that many of them will feel rather badly when they pick up the press to-morrow and find that the minister has raised in this chamber at this time the question of isolationism in Canada. That is all I shall say about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not want to hear another word about isolationism. I want to get on with this war. I want the minister to appreciate the realities and the realism he is talking about. Let us have more positive direction; let us have something with some merit so that we can get on with our war effort. That is the real problem before us. Why should the hon. gentleman rise in his place and make a speech to pave the way for an appointment which apparently was made a day or two ago? That is not reality or realism.
Some of the realities were faced by the minister last night, but he tried to dismiss them in the last paragraph of his speech before he moved that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. He said that the government of this country could not do anything about the matter then under discussion, and he threw a wet blanket over the energetic efforts and enthusiasm of some 25,000 women in Canada who are trying to help the war effort. I refer to
the Canadian women's voluntary services, which was under discussion last night. I am going to make a plea to the minister now, not to close the gate to the energy and efforts of these women who are giving voluntary service. Try to find some way out of the tangle you have let yourself into in following along behind this organization with a paid organization with the same name-the tangle you have got into by order in council-and,
I would not say, usurping the name, but taking away the name which you had previously given to this organization in September, 1941, and by order in council using practically the same name. The name in the order in council to my mind is a misnomer. The order in council says that there shall be a body formed known as the Women's Voluntary Services Division. And the first thing you do is to engage paid help. The first thing you do is to spoil the name "voluntary" entirely by putting on the staff two persons who are paid from the treasury of Canada to do the work which this group of Canadian women have tried to do voluntarily, none of whom- and I ask the minister to mark this carefully -are being paid from funds received by the organization or from the government.
The minister says that the approach of the Canadian women's voluntary services organization is not the approach that he would like to have. Indeed, he says it is the opposite to the approach he wants to have. The minister wants his approach to this problem to come through the present social welfare organizations in Canada. Let us take a broad view of this situation and ask ourselves, who are the social welfare organizations? They are municipal, provincial and dominion bodies doing a good job, and earning their pay as such. But have the women who are at the heads of these social welfare agencies contact with the women of Canada who are giving their voluntary services in this war? Have they the kind of contact with them which will stir women's energies and arouse their patriotism in the form of war work? Some of these women in the difficult times from 1930 to 1940 found it necessary to appeal to the social welfare agencies for help. Not many of them did it, because they did not like to approach the welfare organizations, but a few women through no fault of their own found it necessary during the depression to appeal for assistance to these organizations, and they did so with a sense of humiliation hanging like a cloud around them, and with a sense of defeatism. But they were well treated by the minister's organizations which he now desires to dominate this whole picture. A

War Appropriation-War Services
very large body of women in Canada at that time had a perfect right to appeal to the social welfare organizations for help, but they refrained from doing it. They preferred to suffer in silence and do the best they could. Another very large group of women in Canada, representing probably all the women's organizations that we read about, the council of women, the daughters of the empire, and so forth, rather refrained from going to the social welfare agencies to get leadership in the type of work they would like to do for the war effort. Of course, they will cooperate with the Red Cross and carry out any rules and regulations; but for the minister to say that the approach made by the Canadian women's voluntary services is the direct opposite to the approach he wants to have, his approach being through the welfare organizations, is to put a wet blanket on the enthusiasm and effort of the women to whom I have referred.
What do these women do? They do very much like Lady Reading's organization does in England and similar organizations in the United States and South Africa. They t"ain for home nursing under the Red' Cross, learn creche and child management, act as mother-craft minders, train themselves for home management, take courses in preparedness, learn how to deal with emergencies in war under the direction of the Red Cross, study nutrition. There have been 2,045 classes given, and 2,980 women have completed or are taking these training courses. There have been 200 meetings addressed; 5,000 women have been enrolled and contacts made with 25,000. There are organized disciplined groups of women in each community who are prepared to act in war-time emergencies.
As the hon. member for Peterborough West so well said last night, these women are keen to go on working in a voluntary way. I shall not traverse the ground already covered by the hon. member for Peterborough West and by the hon. member for Lincoln. My plea with the minister is this: Do not stiffen your back on this thing and turn down the representations that are being made by the Canadian women's voluntary services. Let them continue in existence and give some real service to Canada. It is a simple matter for the minister's organization, which comes along afterwards, to say to these women: The government will drop this word "voluntary." Let the minister call his organization by another name, just as he gave names by order in council, dated October 31, to several divisions in his department-the national registration division, the mobilization division, the public information division, the war charities division, the salvage division. Do not use the 
words "women's voluntary services division." Call your organization the women's services division, if you will. Nothing is so hard on anyone, particularly on our womenfolk, as to find that the work they do in their homes and organizations, the knitting they do in every spare hour and late at night, the learning how to be of service in this war cannot go on as it has been going on hitherto, and that a paid staff is to be employed to direct their activities. They do not like the idea of having paid women in these organizations which are called voluntary organizations.
I suggest to the minister that he give very serious consideration to dropping the word "voluntary" which is used in the order in council, and that he encourage the Canadian women's voluntary services to stay in existence. I also urge upon him that he retract the suggestion that the approach of this organization is the opposite to that of the department. Let the view of his department be a little more elastic. Let him encourage the women to continue in existence and carry on the useful work they are doing. By no means discourage them, because in them you have a strong unit of workers, and it will make for a good deal of difficulty if they are washed out, as it were, so far as this particular job is concerned. Mr. Vining has been appointed to do a job in Washington; a woman is the selective service head in Vancouver. Women grow up to responsible paid positions through the social service organizations, and when they come up that way, let us be frank about it, Madam Chairman, and admit that they were nurtured in the cradle of politics right along before they attained to leadership in these different services.
Consider the history of these services. The minister knows it well, although he may be reluctant to cite it for the enlightment of the committee. He will admit that those who are at the heads of these social service organizations have maintained their positions in these organizations through actions which of necessity were political, and which got them into these organizations. That very thought is going to destroy the very idea which we should encourage and foster.

I should like to put the three statements that are attributed to Miss Hyndman side by side with the statements that Mrs. West actually made at the press conference to which Miss Hyndman refers, which was reported in the Globe and Mail of May 12. This statement is made by Miss Hyndman:
1. That the government's plan is to have women's work done in communities by social agencies.
That is not correct. What Mrs. West did say is this:
Mrs. West said that the function of her department is "to unite volunteer war work and civilian services in such a way that the whole volunteer movement marches forward in a coordinated whole on a community basis."
She further explained that the department recommends that in communities having welfare councils, volunteer bureau, or citizens' committees, close cooperation be developed and overlapping, duplication of work, prevented. She also said:
"I am happy to say that Toronto has these facilities already in existence and that the welfare council has already established a bureau on the lines recommended by the department and has made worth-while contributions toward meeting a number of community needs arising out of the war effort. My department will be anxious to assist in its further development and coordination. In a war it is difficult to draw the line between war and home-front services. Peace-time agencies have many wartime duties ami give much advice to soldiers' dependents. It is important in the development of volunteer services to note that there is such a body as the welfare council and council of social_ agencies in existence, because such an organization has an intimate knowledge of community needs and resources and can direct fMr. Thorson.l
volunteer efforts in the channels in which they are most needed. If it works closely with groups engaged in war work, overlapping and duplication will be prevented. It also creates a volunteer structure that will continue as a nation passes from war to peace."
May I say this of the situation in Toronto, that I spent some time there meeting with various organizations, the citizens' committee and then another organization in the afternoon which is deeply concerned with the coordination of the voluntary effort of the citiz.ens of Toronto. I should like to pay tribute to the splendid manner in which the various organizations in Toronto have cooperated with one another in the matter of putting that city on the basis of community solidarity. If a city such as Toronto can do that, with the splendid results that have followed the activities of the organizations in Toronto, then that can be done in other large cities. So that there is a misconception in Miss Hyndman's report of what Mrs. West actually said.
With regard to the second statement attributed to Miss Hyndman and referred to by the hon. member for Peterborough West:
That no war work should be undertaken in a community until these social agencies who have their "ear to the ground as to the needs" give the word "go".
This is what Mrs. West said:
We do not want to stimulate volunteer effort beyond our ability to use it.
Then she went on to say:
There is a danger of making women feel that they are not contributing to the war effort unless they are outside their own homes doing something in a spectacular way. We want people to feel that there is an organization in every community that has its ear to the ground and is prepared to meet emergencies as they arise.
It is not only the women who are wearing uniforms or who are working in a munitions plant or in a war industry who are making contributions to the war effort of Canada. Many of the women who are working in the activities of the community, where there is no glamour, no publicity, no uniform, but only hard work and drudgery, are in my opinion performing at this time a war service of inestimable value. In performing the tasks of the community they are keeping the heart of the community sound'.

munity on what I have termed a basis of community solidarity unless you include in your organizations that are being brought together in a cooperative way those organizations that are concerned with social welfare and social need; for I repeat, they are the core of the community. The third statement that is made, referred to by the hon. member for Peterborough West and likewise attributed to Miss Hyndman is this:
That women should not be trained for emergencies now, nor their free time utilized for war work except such "unspectacular" (as she called them) and relatively unimportant jobs as salvage and price control enforcement. Nor should they be encouraged to organize their lives to have free time which can be so utilized.
What Mrs. West actually did say, as reported in the press, is this:
We do feel that until the job is there to be done women can best serve by looking after their community, keeping a quiet home for a harassed husband to come into at the end of a trying day, helping with the salvage project, and price ceiling, and keeping in touch with the boys in the services here and overseas. There is need in this country to make the seemingly uninteresting jobs seem important to our women. There are only a very few jobs in Canada where there is any glamour! The vast majority of women will have to serve in the war effort in an unobstrusive way.
In so serving, the women of Canada, not concerned with glamour, not concerned with publicity, make a contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort which only they can make; it is a contribution of inestimable value
to this country, because if you do not keep the communities of Canada sound you cannot keep the nation sound. I say this. We have pledged our country to an all-out war effort. There cannot be an all-out war effort unless certain things are done in the communities of Canada. There are many things that must be done in the communities of Canada which can be done only by the men and women of Canada, working voluntarily. There are many things in the communities of Canada which must be done and which no government can do; only the men and the women of the community can do those tasks. If they do not do them, and do them voluntarily, there is not an all-out community effort.

In my view the name Canadian women's voluntary services-

speechtext:
Is it "voluntary" or
"volunteer"?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

There are a number of activities in which this organization could engage. Likewise I do not think it should be permitted to grow into a national organization when there are many existing national organizations doing their tasks effectively. In my opinion the name is not accurately descriptive of the organization. I am quite prepared to grant registration of any fund for which such registration is applied- but under some other name. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would it not be better if they cooperated all round?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think that is the solution. May I say that early in September I met the ladies actively engaged in this organization-Mrs. MacKenzie, Mrs. Conant and Mrs. Bryce-and indicated to them at that time, in Toronto, what the aims of our department were. I pointed out that I did not think they were proceeding in the way which would be most helpful to those aims. They were also advised to the same effect somewhat earlier. The organization sought the blessing of Lady Reading, but Lady Reading would not give it to them. The organization in Great Britain is nation-wide, and the situation there is not the same as it is here.
I assure hon. members that we gave this subject the most careful thought and consulted many people, and that the opinion was almost unanimous that we ought to embark

War Appropriation-War Services
upon a scheme having as its basis the idea of community solidarity. We ought not to try to regiment anyone, but should give guidance and direction, so that the leaders in the community might get together, cooperate with each other, and build their organization on a basis of community solidarity for peacetime social welfare and war-time activities. It was felt that on that basis they could serve the purposes of the community and the nation, and make their utmost contribution to the war effort.
I believe we can find work for these women.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset I wish to associate myself with the observations and suggestions of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George with respect to lack of publicity in the United States respecting Canada and her war effort. I could go back to a time two years ago when I was particularly opposed to the principle of the foreign exchange control board, to that of restricting Canadian travel to the United States, and to the imposition by the United States of passport regulations respecting Canadian citizens. However, that is now water under the bridge.
I have no doubt, however, that those circumstances were the beginning of the rift which has been developing between personal friendships-and I do not mean national friendships-concerning Canadians and citizens of the United States. To counteract that condition it is most necessary that we give our United States friends as much publicity as possible with respect to what Canada has done and is doing in this war.
It has been said that citizens of the United States do not appreciate what we are doing because we have not conscription. I do not intend to discuss that point more than to say that when I addressed a meeting in Watertown, New York, about a month ago, and they heard how many men we have in uniform who are willing to serve the cause of democracy in any part of the world, they were astounded. After the meeting, one after another came to me and said that that was the most gratifying and pleasant news they had heard. They had no idea the condition was such-and Watertown is only twenty-eight miles from the international boundary line.
One peculiar feature in connection with the advertising of an internationally known product is that often an advertisement which will have tremendous appeal in the United States will have none in Canada. The reverse is also true. On many occasions something which will have appeal in Canada will have none in the United States. It has occurred
to me that one of the reasons why we are not putting the story of our war effort across in the United States is that we are not giving it the right appeal. For that reason I agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George that we open a publicity bureau in New York city, and have it headed by the best man who can be chosen from this country. He need not necessarily be a publicity or newspaperman, although I should think a newspaperman would be an excellent choice. But when this office is opened I would suggest the retaining of the services of a first-class United States publicity or advertising agency.
I happen to be associated with a business which does advertising in both Canada and the United States. In Canada we do our advertising through a Canadian agency, but in the United States we use a United States agency because it understands the mass buying psychology of the citizens of that country. I know that United States citizens prefer to have their advertising in forms different from those we have in Canada. They respond more readily to newsreel publicity, and to pictures appearing in newspapers. Are we giving them enough of the kind of advertising they prefer?
May I at this time compliment the Canadian Broadcasting corporation upon the excellence of the international hook-ups carried by the big United States chains. I believe they have done a splendid job.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Do you mean Sister Susan and the like of that? I think that is the most awful stuff I have ever listened to.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
We will leave "Sis" out of it. The point is that we are not going about this thing in the right way. It is vitally necessary that we do this because Canada forms an indivisible bond that links the British empire to the United States of America, and that bond must be stronger to-day than it ever was before. No doubt we are linked closer together because of our common effort in this war of survival than we have ever been before. Living as I do on the international border I realize, however, perhaps more than some who do not live on the border, that as individuals we are growing apart. Nothing in the last year or so has given me greater concern than that.
I hope the few suggestions I have made will be considered and that every effort will be made to publicize from one end of the United States of America to the other just what we are doing over here, what our soldiers, our sailors and our airmen are doing;

War Appropriation-War Services
we should let that country know that our armed forces are prepared to fight in any part of the world. Our airmen to-day are taking part in practically every major battle that occurs. It is an inspiring story, and if properly handled it can be put over in a big way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would the hon. member include in that story the present situation as to national unity in Canada?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think that is a most inopportune statement to make at this time. I do not think that remark should have been made by the leader of the opposition. It is remarks of this kind that make the world believe we are not united.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We certainly have not national unity in this country and never have had. We never will have it under party government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: All I can say is that we hope we are successful in putting over this publicity in a right and proper way.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Prior to coming into this house I worked for a living. I moved in circles where people were doing things. One of my great disillusionments has been to see the way in which serious business is conducted at this time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In the House of Commons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You are wasting time yourself.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am not wasting time, and I shall prove it before I get through. A good deal of time has been wasted this afternoon. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and the last speaker referred to publicity in the United States. I think we are getting too much: there are a lot of things that we have no cause to broadcast or placard across the country. For the past two weeks I have sat here listening to the Minister of National War Services. In my opinion the majority of members of this house have no idea of the functions of that department, and I sometimes doubt whether the minister has. I say that quite frankly. I think I have some idea of the ramifications of the department under the minister's control. I have made some attempt to analyse its activities. When the Prime Minister tabled on March 24 the thirteen orders in council that set up the national selective service organization in this country, the status of this department changed completely.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That is my opinion and I am going to endeavour to prove it. During this

debate the minister has stood in his place and tried to answer questions which belonged rightly to three or four other departments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The Prime Minister's statement is set out on page 1563 of Hansard, and I am going to put that statement on the record again in order that we may discuss the functions of this department as they are related, not only to the calling of men for military service but to the mobilization of the manpower of this country. During the course of the discussion the minister has gone into matters that belonged rightly to the Department of Labour, the Department of Pensions and National Health, and several other departments. These matters will come before the house again at some time in the future and the discussion will be repeated. The Prime Minister said:
The primary responsibility for the extended scheme of national selective service has been placed upon the Minister of Labour. Under the Minister of Labour, the administrative responsibility for the direction and coordination of the policy has 'been vested in a director of national selective service and an associate director. Mr. Elliott M. Little has been appointed the director of national selective service, and Mr. Paul Goulet, the associate director.
The responsibility for increasing the total man-power available for war service has been largely centred in the Department of Labour.
The administrative responsibility for allocating man-power, for placing men and women in the most useful forms of service and for the direction of the women's organizations of this country, has been placed upon the Minister of Labour. The Minister of National War Services has been dealing this afternoon with the women's organizations. The minister took up much time and went to much trouble to analyse a problem that really belongs to another department. The Prime Minister continued:
The other departments of government which share in greater or less degree in the tasks of making man-power available for %var service and in the allocation of the available manpower are the departments of National War Services, Pensions and National Health, Munitions and Supply, Agriculture,-
The responsibility of dealing with men who may be exempt because they are engaged in the agricultural industry is the responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
When the national selective service regulations were brought down there was a change in the status of the calling up of men for military service. Prior to national selective service being adopted the Minister

War Appropriation-War Services
of National War Services called up the proper age groups on the basis of their necessity for military service. When national selective service was set up the emphasis was no longer upon whether a man was eligible for military service, it was upon whether he was essential to a certain war industry.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The national war services regulations are still in my department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister stated a few days ago that they do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That makes the regulations crazier than ever. I had some confidence in the national selective service set-up which was to make plans for distributing our available man-power where it was required in relation to the needs of war production, after I had read some of the speeches that Mr. Little made since his appointment to the head of national selective service.
