I thought he showed a real grasp of the problem; and if Mr. Little were given latitude to organize things in the way he set out in his statements to the press and in his addresses to service clubs, I think he would do well in his position. But it is a different matter entirely if he is to be under the thumb of the Department of Agriculture, the Department of National War Services, the Department of Pensions and National Health and the Department of Labour, and if the complete mobilization of the man and womanpower of this country is still in the hands of a judge and a representative of agriculture. That is the board that is sitting now. I do not know who appointed the representative of agriculture.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member is all mixed up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I listened as carefully as I could to the answers which the minister gave to questions as to the exemption of workers employed in agriculture, and he said that the exemption boards consisted of a judge and two other persons, one of whom was a farmer in the particular case.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not the slightest.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There has been absolutely no trouble with our board. It will be realized as we go along that national selective service is definitely related to the calling up of men for military service; and if Mr. Little is going to function properly, national selective service has to have some representation on the board. As I have said before, the emphasis is no longer upon whether a man is eligible for military service but whether he is essential to war industry, and who is going to decide whether a man is essential to an industry if there is not a national selective service officer on the boards in the different provinces? These boards sit in judgment on a question of life and death, deciding who is to be called up for military service. The national selective service officer in the different provinces is the head of the unemployment insurance office, and ninety-nine out of one hundred of the unemployment insurance officials in every section of Canada have been appointed because of political patronage.

speechtext:
He does not decide
whether a man is to be called for military training.

Who decides?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The divisional boards.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And the national selective
service organization does not come into the picture at all?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They d'o not make that decision.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Here is something that happened this week, and I point it out to show why it is necessary for the national selective service officers to have the major say in who is to be called and who is not to be called.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I understood the hon.
member to say that he did not want them to have the say.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do. I say that the board is not in a position to segregate men into industry and the army and decide who is required for military service, without doing a serious injury to the industries of this country which are necessary to our war production. I have said all along and I repeat it now, that Canada's greatest war effort will be made along the production lines, and not in the field.
Here is a specific case that I wish to bring to the minister's attention. We know that aeroplanes are absolutely necessary on every front, that planes are needed and needed badly. Here is what happened at the de Havilland plant. On the 14th of this month some 400 employees of that plant were called up for military service. Nine of these men were expert tool makers who are essential to the industry and could not be replaced at a moment's notice. None of the men taken from this plant can be replaced inside of sixty days, by men equally efficient. As I say, 400 of these men were called up on the 14th of this month. One of these men, a tool maker, was ordered to go before his own private physician, where he had his blood pressure taken and his heart examined and he was declared Al. . He was given a ticket and sent to Ottawa to report at Connaught ranges. He was given forty-eight hours to do that job in.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Was he a first-class
tool maker?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How old was he?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Twenty-six. He tried to
get a week's extension from the examining board in Toronto so that he could straighten up his affairs, but they had no authority to grant him an extension. These 400 men are being sent to the different camps across Canada. Some of them came to Ottawa. The man to whom I was talking spent a week at Connaught ranges, and then he was reexam-[Mr. Gaiis.l
ined and) declared permanently medically unfit. He has been idle from the 14th to the 29th of this month.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Is he back at the
de Havilland plant?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
He was here in Ottawa to-day and is on his way back to de Havilland.
I say that to take these 400 men out of a very necessary war plant in this country and send them into the armed forces is doing a disservice to this country. Think how serious it is for an aeroplane factory to lose 400 men with experience.
I have three of Mr. Little's speeches here, and I can agree with every word of them. I do not think what I have described would have happened in Toronto if Mr. Little, with the ideas he has expressed, had sat in with that board. I think these 400 men were contributing more to the country's war effort in producing planes for our boys who are out in the field than they could do in pounding a parade ground somewhere in Canada. Armaments and munitions are what we need. That is why I emphasize that if the government had sufficient confidence in Mr. Little, who has a fairly good grasp of what is necessary in the mobilization of workers and of how to relate our man-power needs in industry to our war effort, then instead of involving national selective service with three or four other departments, they would allow Mr. Little and his organization to say who is essential to industry, and his organization should not only be given representation on the board which will handle the call-ups from now on but be given the major say. I would judge from what happened in this case that there is competition; the army wants more men and wants them in a hurry, and perhaps wants them before national selective service gets operating as it should operate and, I believe, as it will operate in the future. As I see it now, the whole question is handled by different departments, and there is nobody with supreme responsibility, nobody in a position to give direction.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There is no coordination.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Somebody has to take hold of the thing and organize it, and I thought that that was Little's job.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend that it will be done-make no mistake about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is an aeroplane plant disrupted right now in Toronto. Take four hundred men out of a plant and it does not do it any good.

War Appropriation-War Services

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: After all is said and done, the facts are not here. A toolmaker is a highly-skilled mechanic. The mere fact that a man says he is a toolmaker does not make him one.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But he has been employed for three years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That may be. We have passed through the stage of the establishment of the regulations, and after some difficulties in Montreal we sent a representative of the national labour supply council as an adviser on the board there. As my hon. friend admitted this afternoon, the boards in his province have been very fair. Whether you and I like it or not we have got to put the women into industry and the young men into the fighting forces. It is not a question of what you want to do, it is a question of what you have got to do. I want first to see the evidence that this man is a toolmaker.
I will agree that while it is comparatively easy to get numbers of majors and colonels, and captains in the navy-I say this with no disrespect to them-it is very difficult to get highly trained toolmakers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then why are you taking them out of industry?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend asks why am I taking them out. I have just pointed out to my hon. friend that first you have to have the evidence; the mere fact that a man tells me that he is a toolmaker does not make him one.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He was employed for three years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is all right. You show me his card and I will tell you whether he is a toolmaker. I know what a toolmaker is. When the war broke out there were-on paper-only 6,300 toolmakers in the whole dominion-I mean persons who said they were toolmakers. I agree that if this man is a toolmaker it is criminal that he should be in the fighting forces. The national labour board has a representative and adviser on the board in Toronto of which this man spoke, and I am doubtful, when the thing comes to be analysed, and the man's card is examined, if it will be shown that the man is a toolmaker.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It is a question of fact.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Of course it is.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I hope the minister is right. But four hundred men were taken out of a shell plant, nine of them being toolmakers
and one a charge hand. If there is a national selective service man on that board in Toronto Mr. Little should take him to task, because certainly he is not acting in accordance with the opinions expressed by Mr. Little in many of these press statements.
The minister says we must put the women into industry. I agree that that should be done when there are no longer any unemployed men in that section who could be used; women should then be trained to take their places in industry in order to fill the places of those who are going into the forces. Those who are charged with the responsibility of organizing this service must see to it that women are not brought into industry for the purpose of reducing wages. I have a letter from Hamilton, signed by the president and the secretary of a union, which says:
Specific cases at present show that male employees at an hourly earning of 80 cents per hour are being replaced by female workers at 33 cents per hour. These male workers are placed on other jobs at rates of 50 cents per hour and a few cases of 574 cents per hour.
We believe these conditions were only to be brought about in case of male employees being called for military purposes.
They thought, as the minister stated a moment ago, it was only when men were called for military service that they would be replaced, and then that the wages should not be reduced. If women are taken in the plant and do the same work which has been done by men, the same wages should be paid. That is a specific case from a Hamilton plant. I hope the minister will see that the matter is checked up.
With respect to the setting up of these boards and the question of exemption and the essentiality of the men to industry, the boards as constituted at the present time are in my opinion not competent to sit in and judge impartially in cases of the kind. Previously they were. It was a straight matter of calling men for military service.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The question raised by the hon. member was just as important before national selective service as it is to-day.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You have had the odd case. To-day you are going to get dozens.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I admit that some will squeeze through the barrier. That happens in all big undertakings such as this.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Four hundred of them?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend says four hundred, but he does not know what he is talking about. Perhaps he will let me finish my statement and we can get along. It was just as essential before selective service that
Royal Canadian Air Force

key men in essential industries should not be called up as it is to-day. The conditions then were just the same as they are now. I say that just to put the matter fairly before the committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The minister is right to a certain extent, but from another point of view he is not. Many industries have been organized in this country during the past year. Practically all the available man-power of the country is either in the armed services or employed in industry; and as the age groups are advanced, when the call goes out for military service most of these people will be coming from either the essential or the non-essential industries. I have letters from several of the steel-workers' organizations. In that industry most of the men are trained for a specific job.
Progress reported.
